title: Josephson spectroscopy in a circular atomic tunnel junction with acceleration-induced symmetry breaking
authors: Yurii Borysenko, Yuriy Bidasyuk, Olena Prykhodko, Gerhard Birkl, Dominik Pfeiffer, Ludwig Lind, Mark Edwards, Alexander Yakimenko
abstract: We study Josephson dynamics in a long atomic Bose-Josephson junction formed by two tunnel-coupled coplanar Bose-Einstein-condensate rings. An in-plane linear acceleration breaks the axial symmetry of the trap and transforms a single Josephson plasma oscillation into a multimode population-imbalance response. Gross-Pitaevskii simulations and Bogoliubov-de Gennes analysis show that the additional spectral components arise from collective modes that acquire finite overlap with the population-imbalance operator under symmetry breaking, with their activation governed by reflection symmetry about the acceleration direction. We also propose a mode-resolved Josephson-spectroscopy protocol based on a weak localized periodic perturbation. Frequency scans reveal resonant amplitude peaks and phase shifts at the eigenfrequencies of active Bogoliubov modes, while angular scans of the drive position provide access to the angular structure of the corresponding mode density perturbations. A dissipative time-dependent Bogoliubov theory yields analytical response functions in quantitative agreement with full Gross-Pitaevskii simulations in the linear regime. Our results demonstrate that accelerated dual-ring condensates provide a controllable platform for symmetry-selected Josephson dynamics and spectroscopic probing of collective modes.
summary: The paper analyzes Josephson dynamics in a double-ring Bose-Einstein condensate subjected to an external linear acceleration. This acceleration breaks the system's axial symmetry, causing the simple plasma oscillation spectrum to become multi-modal. The authors propose a spectroscopic protocol using localized driving fields to selectively measure these newly activated collective Bogoliubov modes.
main_problem: The study investigates how an external linear acceleration breaks the axial symmetry of a Bose-Josephson junction formed by two coupled BEC rings, thereby modifying its Josephson dynamics.
main_result: Acceleration transforms the single Josephson plasma oscillation into a multimode response, activating specific Bogoliubov collective modes whose spectral components can be selectively probed via spectroscopy.
method: The analysis employs Gross-Pitaevskii simulations and Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) theory, proposing a mode-resolved spectroscopic protocol using localized periodic driving perturbations.
model_or_system: The system is a coplanar double-ring trap containing $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms in a BEC. The dynamics are modeled by the GPE, incorporating an external linear acceleration term that breaks rotational symmetry.
key_observables: Population imbalance oscillations ($Z(t)$), Josephson plasma oscillation frequency spectrum, and spectral components corresponding to active Bogoliubov modes.
important_parameters: External acceleration magnitude ($a$), driving frequency ($\omega_d$), and the coupling strength/interaction parameter ($g$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes low-energy dynamics allowing for an effective 2D description, and utilizes linear response theory (BdG) in conjunction with dissipative time-dependent methods.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition from a single spectral peak to a multiplet structure as acceleration increases; they also show mode activity ($D_n$) confirming S-type mode activation and spatial maps of density perturbations ($\deltaho_n$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the baseline Josephson dynamics at zero acceleration, then introducing acceleration to induce symmetry breaking, which is theoretically linked to the activation of specific Bogoliubov modes. Finally, it details a spectroscopic protocol using localized driving fields to selectively measure these activated modes.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, controllable platform (accelerated BECs) to experimentally realize and spectroscopically probe fundamental concepts like symmetry-protected degeneracies and mode coupling in many-body quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the dual-ring Bose Josephson junction. (a) Two coaxial toroidal condensates separated by a barrier that supports coherent tunneling between the rings, together with an additional time-dependent potential used to perturb the system. (b) The density modulation of a Bogoliubov mode that becomes active in the population-imbalance dynamics. Arrows indicate the direction of the tunneling flow across the barrier.

FIG. 2. Time evolution of the population imbalance Z(t) (top row) and the corresponding Fourier spectra (bottom row) for three values of the acceleration: a = 0 (left column), a = 10 mm/s2 (middle column), and a = 20 mm/s2 (right column). For a nonzero acceleration, Z(t) exhibits a pronounced beating pattern, indicating the presence of several active oscillation frequencies. In the Fourier spectra, the single dominant Josephson peak observed at a = 0 evolves into a multiplet structure whose components shift with increasing acceleration.

FIG. 4. Spatial structure of the lowest Bogoliubov modes active in the population-imbalance dynamics, represented by the density perturbation δρn defined in Eq. (17). The rows correspond to a = 0 (top), 5 mm/s2, 10 mm/s2, 15 mm/s2, and 20 mm/s2 (bottom). With increasing acceleration, the mode profiles become progressively distorted and asymmetric, consistent with the growth of their activity in Fig. 5 and with the associated changes in the tunneling dynamics.

FIG. 3. Elementary-excitation spectrum as a function of the applied acceleration a. Solid red lines represent modes sym- metric with respect to the x axis (labeled Sn), while dashed blue lines represent antisymmetric modes (labeled An). The zero-frequency Goldstone mode is labeled S0. The mode la- beled J is the principal Josephson mode discussed in the text. For a > 0, symmetry breaking activates additional modes in the population-imbalance dynamics, leading to the multiplet structure seen in Fig. 2. Black crosses denote the peak fre- quencies extracted from the dynamical simulations.
